comment.value: The reviewers all like the line of research and find the results interesting. The submission nicely combines multi-objective optimization with the framework of data-driven algorithms. The main point of the discussion was if the methods are novel enough to meet the bar for ICML. While the general framework for bounding the sample complexity is by now standard, the main novelty is in Sections 5 and 6 and consists in applying smoothed analysis to the problem in question. This is a nice twist but also in these sections the methods seem quite related to previous work on smoothed analysis. Overall, the submission contains interesting results even though the technical novelty is somewhat debatable.

Thanks for your comment.

> It seems that the results of Section 3.1 are not novel, but the situation requiring multiple parameters is novel. On the other hand, the main contribution is said to be in the smoothed analysis bounding the number of pieces, but I see in another review that this is limited to the case of two objectives.

We kindly clarify that this is not a contradiction. Perhaps there is a misunderstanding regarding "multiple parameters". By "learning $k$ parameters" in Section 3.1, we mean that we learn a portfolio of configurations so that we can build a Pareto set, instead of learning only a single configuration. Although an algorithm for a two-objective optimization problem may have only one parameter (i.e., the notation $d$ in Section 2, problem formulation), we learn "multiple" values for this parameter (i.e., the notation $k$ in Section 2) to form a configuration portfolio since there is usually no universal optimal solution for both objectives. This is stated in the problem formulation in Section 2.

For example, as in our experiments in Section 7.2, although SALT has only one parameter, we learn $k$ values of the parameter to optimize the Pareto volume. Thus, Section 3.1 is not contradictory to the limitation of the two-objective case.

> Much of the paper's framing seems targeted at generic optimization problems, but it later becomes clear that it only applies to discrete optimization having a piecewise-constant structure.

We admit that our analysis cannot apply to every multi-objective optimization problem. It is also impossible to achieve a tight generalization bound for generic optimization problems, considering the diverse structures of different algorithms. However, we do believe the piecewise structure, shared by approximation algorithms, local search, linear programs, and MDPs, is a quite general framework that covers a wide range of multi-objective optimization problems.

comment.value:
I appreciate the clear and thorough answers to my questions. I admit that I do not understand the finer points of the proof strategies or their novelty.

It seems that the results of Section 3.1 are not novel, but the situation requiring multiple parameters is novel. On the other hand, the main contribution is said to be in the smoothed analysis bounding the number of pieces, but I see in another review that this is limited to the case of two objectives. Much of the paper's framing seems targeted at generic optimization problems, but it later becomes clear that it only applies to discrete optimization having a piecewise-constant structure. 

It seems that the question of novelty and significance in this paper is full of subtlety. Overall, I'm still unable to push for acceptance on my end, because I'm not able to convince myself the significance of the technical advancement, within the larger literature.

Thanks for your review! We are delighted that you consider our work thorough and comprehensive. We address your concerns as follows:

> Q: How novel are the theoretical results of Section 3.1? Are they very general beyond the setting of multiobjective discrete optimization?

We admit that the results in Section 3.1 are not technically novel. As discussed in the paper, the piecewise-constant structure has appeared in previous work, e.g., Gupta & Roughgarden (2017), Balcan et al. (2018a, 2021a). The difference is that we need to learn multiple parameters in multiobjective optimization (MOO), while in previous work, only one parameter is required (and this is where our analysis is related to MOO).

However, we want to emphasize that we introduce the results in Section 3.1 only because it is the basis of subsequent analysis. The main technical novelty of our work is the subsequent bounds on the number of pieces in this structure (especially Sections 5 & 6). We use smoothed analysis to reduce the worst-case exponential bounds to polynomial sizes for local search and linear programs, which are highly non-trivial compared with previous work.

For example, Balcan et al. (2018a) study the generalization bound of selecting branching parameters for integer programming (IP). They prove the number of pieces for the branching parameter is $O(2^{n(n-1)/2}n^n)$, and this gives an $O(n^2)$ pseudo-dimension / Rademacher complexity bound for IPs with $n$ variables. This bound is very loose (e.g., it requires over $10^6$ samples to obtain a non-vacuous generalization bound). However, in our work, although the number of pieces can be exponential in the worst-case, it can be reduced to polynomial under a slight random noise for local search and linear programs (and this matches empirical results). Thus, **logarithmic** Rademacher complexity bounds are achieved. We believe this phenomenon is very interesting since similar results have not appeared in other data-driven algorithmic settings, and this is the key contribution of our work.

> Q: Is the algorithm for Pareto volume optimization novel, or just the guarantees?

We agree that submodular maximization is a classic algorithm and is applied to many machine learning tasks, such as feature selection [1]. However, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that applies submodular optimization to parameter selection of MOO problems.

Another thing that we want to point out is that ERM is seldom discussed in previous work of data-driven algorithm design. The only work is [2] and its method is not very practical. Thus, although proving the submodularity of Pareto volume is not technically fancy, we believe it is interesting to present our ERM method in the paper, considering its application in practice (Section 7.2).

[1] Bilmes. Submodularity In Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence. arXiv 2202.00132.  
[2] Balcan et al. Accelerating ERM for data-driven algorithm design using output-sensitive techniques. NeurIPS-2024.

> Q: I wish the paper were more friendly to beginners in statistical learning theory, because despite being greatly interested in data-driven optimization, the paper left me questioning how interesting I should find this intersectional topic.

Thanks for your valuable advice! Since we want to make our presentation of main results rigorous and comprehensive, we spend much space on discussing settings of our results, and only discuss the intuition of using statistical learning theory to study MOO in Section 1. We will modify it to include more intuitive discussions (if accepted). We clarify as follows to make our contributions clear:

Briefly speaking, statistical learning theory answers the question of why machine learning models can generalize to unseen data in training. A tight generalization bound is important since it implies the number of data samples such that the learned model does not overfit training data and has strong generalization abilities.

The same question also arises in algorithm configuration. In practice, we just tune the parameter of MOO algorithms on sampled instances, and select a configuration that performs good on these instances. But why does this parameter generalize?

Our work answers this question by showing that the size of the piecewise-constant structure is small. Thus, the learned parameters for MOO can generalize since the intrinsic complexities of these MOO algorithms are limited. From the practical view, our logarithmic generalization bound indicates that the number of instances required for training is only **logarithmic** as the problem size grows. From the theoretical view, our results are interesting, since it is somewhat surprising that classic learning theory, (together with smoothed analysis) is also able to shed light on algorithm configuration with **discrete** algorithmic structures.

We hope that the above responses make the positioning of our paper more clear with our contributions clarified.

Thanks for your review! We are delighted that you consider our work sound and rigorous. We address your concerns as follows:

> Q: Does the proposed theoretical framework for data-driven multiobjective optimization offer any practical insights?

This is a very good question. In this work, we use statistical learning theory to study the generalization ability of multi-objective optimization (MOO) algorithms. Briefly speaking, statistical learning theory answers the question of why machine learning models are able to generalize to unseen data in training. A tight generalization bound is important since it implies the number of data samples such that the learned model does not overfit training data and has strong generalization abilities.

The same question also arises in algorithm configuration. In MOO, we just tune the parameter of MOO algorithms on sampled problem instances, and select a configuration that performs good on these instances in practice. But why does this parameter generalize? Our work answers this question by showing that the size of the piecewise-constant structure is small. Thus, the learned parameters for MOO can generalize since the intrinsic complexities of these MOO algorithms are limited. From the practical view, our logarithmic generalization bound (w.r.t. problem sizes) indicates that the number of problem instances required for training is only **logarithmic** as the problem size grows.

Moreover, our empirical risk minimization method for Pareto volume in Section 3.2 is actually practical. As we show in experiments of Section 7.2, the ERM method indeed improves the Pareto volume (although the $1-1/e$ approximation ratio may be loose in practice).

> Q: The smoothed analysis is restricted to the two-objective case.

This is indeed a limitation of our analysis. Still, we emphasize that the smoothed analysis for two objectives in our paper is already non-trivial compared with previous work. For example, Balcan et al. (2018a) studies the generalization bound of selecting branching parameters for branch-and-bound solvers. They prove that the number of pieces for the branching parameter is $O(2^{n(n-1)/2}n^n)$, and this gives an $O(n^2)$ pseudo-dimension / Rademacher complexity bound for integer programs with $n$ variables. This bound is very loose (e.g., it requires over $10^6$ samples to obtain a non-vacuous generalization bound). However, in our work, although the number of pieces can be exponential in the worst-case, it can be reduced to polynomial under a slight random noise for local search and linear programs (and this matches empirical results). Thus, logarithmic Rademacher complexity bounds (w.r.t. problem sizes) are achieved. We believe this phenomenon is very interesting since similar results have not appeared in other data-driven algorithmic settings.

Moreover, the case of two objectives has already covered many applications of MOO in practice, e.g., the reference Yang et al. (2023) in our paper. Thus, our analysis is compatible with practice.

> Q: It would be good to validate all the algorithms discussed in Sections 4, 5, and 6 in the experiments section.

Thanks for your advice! Since the primary area of our paper is learning theory, we put much attention to theoretical results in our work. We will include more experimental results in the appendix (if accepted).

We hope that the above responses make the positioning of our paper more clear with our contributions clarified.

Thanks for your review! We answer your question as follows:

> Q: Since the title is multi-objective optimization (instead of combinatorial multi-objective optimization) while the discussions in the paper seem mostly focus on combinatorial optimization, can the proposed method be applied to continuous multi-objective black box optimization algorithms (i.e., MOEA/D or NSGA-III) which may not have piecewise-constant structures?

This is a very good question!

First, in Section 6.1 we focus on generalization results for general linear programs. Linear programming is not usually considered as a combinatorial optimization problem (and this is why we say multi-objective optimization (MOO) instead of combinatorial MOO in the title).

Second, generalization bounds for the configuration of black-box optimization algorithms are indeed an interesting direction for future research. Sadly, due to the black-box nature of these problems (which means the landscape of the performance metric function is unknown), the behavior of these algorithms may go arbitrarily ill without reasonable assumptions. We do not have substantial mathematical tools to tackle them. In future work, we will explore whether some mild assumptions can yield meaningful generalization guarantees.

> Q: How is the time efficiency of the proposed method, i.e., comparing to the vanilla geometric series in SALT?

The time overhead is rather mild compared with vanilla parameter settings. For the ICCAD-15 benchmark, the number of pieces is usually only between 2 to 5 for most instances. Since we use binary search to find the pieces of each instance, the ERM method is very efficient. It costs about 23 minutes for the complete ERM and evaluation process, while the vanilla method has already required about 19 minutes to run all instances (for the extreme case of $k=12$).

> Q: In Appendix A authors present the review of related works. However, for algorithm configuration and machine learning for multi-objective optimization, some related works are not included, especially black-box optimization works.

Thanks for pointing out the missing references! We will include them in the paper (if accepted). Still, just to clarify, we remark that the generalization bound results in our work are based on **uniform convergence**, which is independent of the learning algorithm. Thus, these results hold for **any algorithm configurators** that are used.

> Q: Although the authors provide comprehensive proofs for the proposed method, the performance comparison in the experiment only includes the application on SALT with two-objective problems, while more algorithms and problems with more objectives are not rigorously evaluated.

We clarify that the contributions of our sample complexity results include two parts: Section 3.1 focuses on the uniform convergence generalization bounds, which is independent of the ERM algorithm. It holds for any algorithm configurators and any performance metric functions. Section 3.2 focuses on the special case that the performance metric is the Pareto volume. In this case, we present an efficient ERM method to select the parameters.

Experiments in Section 7.1 are conducted to verify the results in Section 3.1 (local search and MDP), while Section 7.2 focuses on the ERM method (SALT). Section 7.1 is also very important, since they are conducted to verify the effectiveness of smoothed analysis for local search and linear programs. The results in Section 7.1 show that the number of pieces in the piecewise structure grows moderately as we increase the problem size. This shows that the smoothed analysis setting is reasonable and is compatible with practice (which is a key contribution of our work). In Section 7.2, we evaluate the ERM method on the SALT algorithm since the Pareto curves are generally applied to evaluate the shallow-light Steiner tree algorithms as in Chen & Young (2020).

We hope that the above responses make the positioning of our paper clearer with our contributions clarified.

Thanks for your review! We are delighted that you considered our work clearly organized and logical. We answer your question as follows:

> Q: The proof assumes the piecewise-constant structure holds for all instances, but this paper does not discuss how to verify it. This property is crucial to bound the algorithm's complexity.

We want to clarify that the piecewise-constant structure (Definition 3.1) is not an **assumption**, but a **condition** of our framework in Section 3.1. The algorithms we analyze in Sections 4, 5, and 6 all satisfy this condition as in our proofs.

> Q: Theorem 3.6 assumes an oracle to compute each piece of $\mathcal{A}$. A more detailed discussion of the oracle in the practical implementation would be better provided to enhance clarity. How this could be relaxed or approximated in real-world applications.

Thanks for your suggestion! In Appendix E (line 1119 of page 21), we discuss how to compute the number of pieces in this structure experimentally (i.e., the oracle in Theorem 3.6). Starting from zero (if the parameter lies in $[0,1]$), we use binary search to find the breaking point of the current piece, and iteratively do this for each piece we found. We will add a remark after Theorem 3.6 to enhance clarity (if accepted).

> Q: For Appendix D, the extension seems to lack discussion on feature selection, model choice (linear, neural nets).

Let us clarify our result in Appendix D.1: Theorem D.1 is a general result. It holds for **any features** $\theta$ and **any prediction model** with a finite pseudo-dimension $d$. For example, if the model is the linear regression with $F$ features, then $d=F$. If the model is a ReLU neural network with $W$ weights and $L$ layers, then $d=O(WL\log W)$ [1].

[1] Bartlett et al. Nearly-tight VC-dimension and pseudodimension bounds for piecewise linear neural networks. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 2019.

We hope that the above responses make the positioning of our paper clearer with our contributions clarified.

summary.value:
This paper proves generalization guarantees for the problem of selecting a weighting parameter in multiobjective optimization. Then, it proves the PAC-learnability of parameters which maximize the Pareto volume in polynomial time. It adapts these results to several classes of optimization problems.

## Update after author response
Regarding the authors' last comment, I agree there is no such contradiction within the paper's claimed contributions. My main point was that appreciating its essential, novel contributions requires much discernment between the proposed and previously existing work, as well as between the preface material (which is framed pretty generally) and the more limited scope which is ultimately delivered on. Overall I don't have the confidence to push for acceptance, but would not oppose it.

claims_and_evidence.value: The evidence comes mainly in the proofs. I'm not qualified to validate the correctness of the proofs, but I believe all the evidence is sound to the best of my understanding.

methods_and_evaluation_criteria.value: The paper seems to propose a method for the ERM optimization of the weighting parameter, based on well-known submodular optimization, but I cannot tell how novel is the method itself. Otherwise the paper proposes no new methods, but focuses on provable theoretical results.

theoretical_claims.value: All the proofs are relegated to the appendix; I have read through their organization but did not check the details. I don't detect any major faults.

experimental_designs_or_analyses.value: The experimental context of the paper is quite sparse, consisting of a figure which corroborates the generalization bounds, and a table which reports accuracy of the proposed ERM. I don't see any issues with the results.

relation_to_broader_scientific_literatur.value: The paper is at the intersection of statistical learning theory and data-driven optimization.

other_strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
I think the paper does a rather thorough job of what it sets out to do: proving error bounds around the problem of learning an optimal objective weight in multi-objective optimization. It also does a good job of relating how those abstract results can be applied to optimization problems of specific forms. For readers interested in these specific questions, I believe this paper provides comprehensive answers. 

My only concern is how significant the results really are, to those who would be interested. From what I can gather, almost none of the analysis before Section 3.2 seems to depend on the fact that were are studying multi-objective optimization. It seems to mostly follow from the piecewise-constant property, which should be satisfied by any number of parameter selection problems for discrete algorithms, not just multiobjective optimization. I'm not positioned to tell how novel is this material. 

The ERM method for Pareto volume maximization by submodular optimization is pretty interesting, but again I cannot tell how novel is the idea itself, or if the novelty lies in the theoretical guarantee.

other_comments_or_suggestions.value: The paper is tightly structured to present all the results in a very organized way, which makes it easy to navigate around. On the other hand, much back and forth navigation was necessary for me, since the paper wastes very little space to motivate the intuitive significance of each result. I won't presume to suggest this is a flawed organization, but I feel it puts much onus on the reader to find their own reasons to be interested in the results. I wish the paper were more friendly to beginners in statistical learning theory, because despite being greatly interested in data-driven optimization, the paper left me questioning how interesting I should find this intersectional topic.

questions_for_authors.value:
- Is the algorithm for Pareto volume optimization novel, or just the guarantees?
- How novel are the theoretical results of Section 3.1? Are they very general beyond the setting of multiobjective discrete optimization?
- If so, why do they not already exist in the literature?

summary.value: This paper establishes the theoretical foundation of data-driven multi-objective optimization. Authors discuss the piecewise structure of combinatorial optimization algorithms and prove a theorem which bounds the sample complexity of parameterized multi-objective combinatorial optimization algorithms. Authors then analyse the application of the proposed theorem on several algorithms and experimental results validate the effectiveness of the propsoed method on  multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems.

claims_and_evidence.value: The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on configuring parameters for different approximation algorithms, local search methods and linear programing methods on multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems in the experiments.

methods_and_evaluation_criteria.value: The authors present the detailed proof of the proposed theorems and methods in the paper and appendix, experimental results also validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, which makes sense.

theoretical_claims.value: The authors provide the detailed proof of the proposed theorems, lemmas and claims in the Appendix one by one.

experimental_designs_or_analyses.value: The authors discuss the changing of the number of pieces and generalization errors of local search and MDP methods along the problem size. The superior performance of the proposed method configured SALT over vanilla SALT is demonstrated. However, the performance of the local search and LP methods configured by the proposed method is not evluated.

supplementary_material.value: Appendix A presents the review of related works. However, for algorithm configuration and machine learning for multi-objective optimziation, some related works are not included. Appendix B is the preliminaries for multi-objective optimization and learning theory. The proofs for the proposed theorems, lemmas and claims are presented in Appendix C, while the extension theorems on parameter predictors and optimization scenarios with more than two objectives are demonstrated in Appendix D. Appendix E shows more experimental details/

relation_to_broader_scientific_literatur.value:
1) Algorithm Configuration: The proposed theorems and method are used to configure tunable paremeters of algorithms.

2) Multi-objective optimization: The proposed method is applied to solve multi-objective optimization problems.

essential_references_not_discussed.value:
In Appendix A authors present the review of related works. However, for algorithm configuration and machine learning for multi-objective optimziation, some related works are not included, especially black-box optimization works. For instance, MADAC[1] published in NeurIPS 2022 uses multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for algorithm configuration on multi-objective optimziation algorithm, similar works include RLMODE[2], MRL-MOEA[3] and so on. I recommend referring to an ArXiv survey[4] which provides more machine learning based algorithm configuration works for multi-objective optimziation.

[1] Xue, Ke, et al. "Multi-agent dynamic algorithm configuration." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (2022): 20147-20161.

[2] Yu, Xiaobing, et al. "Reinforcement learning-based differential evolution algorithm for constrained multi-objective optimization problems." Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence 131 (2024): 107817.

[3] Wang, Jing, et al. "A novel multi-state reinforcement learning-based multi-objective evolutionary algorithm." Information Sciences 688 (2025): 121397.

[4] Ma, Zeyuan, et al. "Toward Automated Algorithm Design: A Survey and Practical Guide to Meta-Black-Box-Optimization." arXiv preprint arXiv:2411.00625 (2024).

other_strengths_and_weaknesses.value: Weakness: Although the authors provide comprehensive proofs for the proposed method, the performance comparison in the experiment only includes the application on SALT with two-objective problems, while more algorithms and problems with more objectives are not rigorously evaluated.

questions_for_authors.value:
1) Since the title is multi-objective optimization (instead of combinatorial multi-objective optimization) while the discussions in the paper seem mostly focus on combinatorial optimization, can the proposed method be applied to continuous multi-objective black box optimization algorithms (i.e., MOEA/D or NSGA-III) which may not have piecewise-constant structures?

2) How is the time efficiency of the proposed method, i.e., comparing to the vanilla geometric series in SALT?

summary.value: This paper provides a generalization framework for data-driven multi-objective optimization through sample complexity analysis. The smoothed analysis offers logarithmic bounds, making the framework feasible for real-world problems. If the performance metric is Pareto volume, this paper further shows that an approximately optimal configuration can be PAC-learned. The proposed framework is then applied to various problems including local search, linear programming, MDP, etc. Numerical results also support the smoothed analysis assumption.

claims_and_evidence.value:
Most claims are supported by clear evidence.

Theorem 3.6 assumes an oracle to compute each piece of $\mathcal{A}(\cdot, I)$. A more detailed discussion of the oracle in the practical implementation would be better provided to enhance clarity. How this could be relaxed or approximated in real-world applications.

methods_and_evaluation_criteria.value: The benchmarks including Shallow-light Trees, Local Search, and synthetic MDPs are common domains for multi-objective optimization. The Pareto volume is a standard metric for multi-objective optimization. Both the benchmark datasets and performance metrics make sense for the proposed method. However, the restriction to only two objectives limits the applicability to higher-dimensional situations. It would be better to provide some empirical demonstration, not just the discussion in Appendix D.

theoretical_claims.value: The proof assumes the piecewise-constant structure holds for all instances, but this paper does not discuss how to verify it. This property is crucial to bound the algorithm's complexity.

experimental_designs_or_analyses.value: Figure 3 shows the number of discontinuities/number of pieces and generalization error as functions of problem size, demonstrating the smoothed complexity bound.

supplementary_material.value: For Appendix D, The extension seems to lack discussion on feature selection, model choice (linear, neural nets).

relation_to_broader_scientific_literatur.value: This paper connects multi-objective optimization and data-driven design by introducing piecewise-constant structure and smoothed analysis.

essential_references_not_discussed.value: As far as I know, all the essential related works are cited and discussed. It would be better to provide more details on the piecewise constant structure.

other_strengths_and_weaknesses.value: This paper is clearly organized, with a logical progression from theoretical framework to applications and numerical results.

other_comments_or_suggestions.value: I do not have any other comments.

questions_for_authors.value: All my concerns are presented above.

title.value: Learning Configurations for Data-Driven Multi-Objective Optimization

TLDR.value: We provide learning-theoretic foundations of algorithm configuration for multi-objective optimization algorithms.

abstract.value: Multi-objective optimization problems arise widely in various fields. In practice, multi-objective optimization is generally solved by heuristics with tunable parameters that are highly application-specific. Tuning parameters based on real-world instances (a.k.a. algorithm configuration) are generally empirical without theoretical guarantees. In this work, we establish the theoretical foundation of data-driven multi-objective optimization through the lens of machine learning theory. We provide generalization guarantees on selecting parameters for multi-objective optimization algorithms based on sampled problem instances. Moreover, if the performance metric of the algorithm is the Pareto volume, we can PAC-learn the approximately optimal configuration in polynomial time. We apply our framework to various algorithms, including approximation algorithms, local search, and linear programming. Experiments on multiple problems verify our theoretical findings.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.now())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.now().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
